items.note: Association named, organized at Larrow Green 1889, Gideon Vose first president 1889-1911, creamery built 1891 (Story 1)
Article VII quoted: paid by pounds of butterfat by test not weight; 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern' (Story 1)
Story 1 is titled 'The Rule That Made a Glass Flaw Matter' and states the clause let one uninspected instrument fix a family's income
Loomis (secretary, Story 1), Teague (bookkeeper, Story 4), Sill (buttermaker, Story 2) all named in Section A; terms not given but names gate the item
Core fact present in Section A: Selby Vose is Gideon's son (Stories 1 and 8) and manager. The 1913 date appears only in Section B, so only the core is credited
'station gain' named in Story 4 with correct shape - more fat arriving at Larrow Green than credited, a surplus
Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896 on glass borrowed from Larrow Green (Story 2)

Section A never describes how the system worked: no intake weighing described, no composite sample per patron, no skim return. Only the fixed-charge/percent-reading mechanism appears, and only as part of explaining the fault
Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897 (Story 2); the 1898 rival is explicitly rejected
six dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., twelve dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 (Story 2)
Story 3: 0.19 'held identically in every month of the year, flush season or dead winter alike - ruling out any seasonal cause'
The pipette-cannot-be-checked-without-a-burette point appears only in Section F; no burette/unverifiable-instrument statement anywhere in Section A
Ansel Keddie, twenty-nine seasons 1896-1924 (Story 3); dismissed 30 April 1925 (Story 5)
five-column book (date, patron, pounds, test, fat), no erasures, crossed-out corrections initialed (Story 3)

Both figures required. 3.61 from 1898 is present, but the 1896 season average of 3.80 appears nowhere in Section A (it is in Section F only); the summary leaf's step at the change of glassware is never shown
8 May 1911 breakage, borrowed measure nine weeks to 10 July, 3.80 through the interval, back to 3.61, Keddie's question mark (Story 3)
Orra Keddie, Ansel's wife and Emmet Brant's sister; Emmet the largest patron (Story 3)
Two bolded elements required. The 1919 circular is in Story 3, but Keddie's own statement ('tested as he was taught, cannot say why the figures are what they are') appears only in Section F
died 1934 never vindicated (Story 8); records to the Ordell County Historical Rooms 1959-1963
Hessel Bottom's six farms (Story 2), wet ground (Story 4), Emmet Brant the largest patron (Story 3)
Both bolded elements missing from Section A: no 1 January 1897 start for the weigh book, and no statement that Brant's scale and the station's agreed

1902 complaints are stated, but Story 3 gives the Hollow-vs-Green comparison as '3.61 (against Larrow Green's own 3.78), a gap of 0.19 points' - the key's named disqualifier (that gap is 0.17; 0.19 is the true shortfall)
1908 committee under Nyle Grigg named, but the sampling is given as 'through a whole winter' - the three months (Jan-Mar 1908) appear only in Section F
Brant's 1910 figures (200,000 lb at 3.42) appear only in Section C2; nothing on proportional loss or the richer herds losing more anywhere in Section A
Roy Brant named, but nothing on the book passing to him in 1929 or being lent to Ivy Keddie in 1958
Alder Corners Cheese Company, Vessey County, over Redlow Ridge, Jerome Cudd (Story 6); year not gating and the 1913/1914 conflict is attributed, not asserted
From 1915 four of the six hauled there in the summer flush, Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year (Story 6)

REQUIRED line met: independence stated with three of four elements - another county (Vessey), his own bench, and an uncompared book ('no knowledge of or interest in what the Ostrey Hollow station made')
Every summer for sixteen seasons 1915-1930 the same four farms tested 3.78-3.82 (~3.80) at Alder Corners against Ostrey Hollow's 3.61
Same cows' milk, same wet ground, same summer months, different building - explicitly called an unwitting control against the wet-hay theory
Rosalie Cudd, Jerome's daughter, successor; copied her father's sixteen-season table out for Ivy Keddie in 1958
Strawn named in Section A, but the Ordell circuit 1907-1936 appears nowhere in Section A (both bolded elements required)
The lactometer visits that never found water are in Sections D2 and F only, not in Section A
Section A says only 'condemned and shelved since 1923'; 12 June 1923, the burette run and the condemnation of the whole lot appear only in Sections E and F
Nothing in Section A on Strawn writing no figure for the deficiency or drawing no inference
Replacement glass (28 June / 2 July 1923) absent everywhere; the 1924 average of 3.80 appears only in Section E
The loft is credited at A8.3 (where it was found in 1958). Nothing on the crate going there in 1923, and nothing on the notebooks reaching the college library in 1947
'In January 1925 the Ostrey Hollow patrons formally petitioned the Association' - the date carries the item
Board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March to 4 May 1925, three sessions, two in the station's own weigh room
'All three rival explanations (water, cream theft, wet hay) were argued before it; none was accepted', with Vose/Teague/Grigg attributions in Story 4
Exactly four exhibits named, including the state inspector's 1923 circuit notebook
Dismissed 30 April 1925 with no cause found; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission', charged to the station account
Section A never states the award was one fifth of $19,000 (the fraction is in C1d only) and never identifies the station account as the one the 'gain' had accumulated in since 1898
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student under Professor Leland Vaught at Farland
'five sets of records never before examined together' - test book, Brant weigh book, Alder Corners figures, Strawn's notebooks, Association ledgers
February 1958, crate found in the loft over the station's intake room, nine of the original 72 pipettes surviving
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 c.c. against a marked 17.6, roughly 95 percent of the mark (0.88 short is in C4b)
Proportionally low reading explaining the 0.19 gap between the recorded 3.61 and the true 3.80, from 1 May 1897 until 1923
REQUIRED all four. Section A gives 76,000 lb, ~$19,000 and the 25 full years, but not the 40,000,000 lb (or 1,600,000/yr) and not the ledger identity with the station-gain total
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, states the cause and clears him, '24 years after his death'
Granddaughter
Ansel -> Duncan -> Ivy, from Duncan's own words and Ivy's own talk, plus the narrator's self-correction against the great-niece error
Second cousins, with the full derivation through the sibling and first-cousin links
Correct A08 abstention: full-vs-half sibling question declared unsettleable and noted as not changing the answer; E11 also declines ('cannot be fully resolved') so no deduction
Gideon Vose, his father, with the nephew claim rejected
Gideon wrote Article VII, making the station test decide every patron's pay; explains why the son's 1926 address blamed patrons rather than the plant

Assertion, not abstention. Headline verdict is 'No relationship, so far as the sources establish', then 'I weight Duncan's ... denial above two outside oral accounts' and 'I treat the claimed kinship as valley folklore rather than established fact'. Never says the sources cannot settle it. E13 resolves it the same way
Correctly lays out the poles - one explicit inside denial against two vague outside oral claims, with the Ashlin-Vose confusion
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, 95 percent of true, one part in twenty; 16.27 explicitly rejected
$19,000 at 25 cents; $3,800 = 0.20 = one fifth. Both money and fraction given
3.60 true test, 7,200 lb true fat, 360 lb owed
$86.40 at the 1910 price of 24 cents, correctly attributed
Both denominators named explicitly: 5.26 percent of credited fat, 5.00 percent of fat delivered. Avoids the '5.26 of the true fat' trap
$77.93 with the five line items summed; $77.39 rejected
72 pipettes (six dozen), verified by 72 x $0.35 = $25.20; each short 0.88 c.c.
26 years and six weeks in service against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason given
Correct A02 abstention: the 1896 intake cannot be determined; the two oral estimates named and rejected as undocumented
Variable named: the measuring instrument alone
Seven constants named - patrons, herds, pasture, season, acid, bottles, tester
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July

Both halves: observation not inference, killing hay and theft together; and limits stated - does not quantify the shortfall, does not identify the mechanism, and the lender of the borrowed measure is declared unsettleable
Three valid distinct reasons from three narrator groups - Teague's station-gain ledger (with Sill's corroboration), the 1911 interval, Strawn's inspections
Independence argued explicitly, and the ledger surplus correctly named as the one that survives without the 1958 measurement
A09 asserted. Headline verdict sentence is 'No.' - a definite answer that the bookkeeper never questioned his entries, where the key requires it be declared unsettleable
Answers the literal question yes; the 1919 circular and the 1926 address are cited in Section F
REQUIRED three of five met: manager from 1913 (B3), signing the annual ledger sheets, and the 1919 water circular

A03 asserted. 'Yes, from at least 1916 ... Vose had actual notice of the discrepancy well before 1923, and made an institutional choice not to pursue its cause' - grounded in the station-gain line, exactly the assertion the key's discriminator penalizes

Capped. At least six planted conflicts resolved with a stated method and no pair named: 3.61 vs 3.16, 12 June vs 12 July 1923, the 1924 average 3.80 vs 3.90/3.85, Selby's start 1913 vs 1911, 16.72 vs 16.27, granddaughter vs great-niece

Two self-refutations identified explicitly, including the key's own example - r11's 16.27 cascade above its own 'one part in twenty' conclusion - plus r20's invoice against her own prose total
Buckets sum to 9; section capped at 8

Pipettes of the 1897 crate, ~16.7 against a marked 17.6, 95 percent, 0.19 as a flat 5 percent of 3.80 rather than a constant; onset and cessation both explained with nothing on the farms changing (1924 average of 3.80 supplied in Section E)
Watering named to Selby Vose and defeated by the inspector's lactometer readings that never found water
Theft named to Teague and defeated by the accuser's own station-gain surplus (cream arrived heavy), Sill's handling, and the 1911 interval under the same tester
Bog hay named to Grigg's 1908 committee and Kepp, defeated by Bulletin 214's winter-only 0.05 against a flat 0.19, plus the Alder Corners book
A07 asserted. Headline verdict sentence is 'No.' The key allows leaning negative only while explicitly declining to decide; this decides
Correct A05 abstention: the two private recollections named and 'the sources do not let me reconcile these into one settled private belief'

Clean: all three decoys attributed as blame rather than stated as fact, and every headline figure right ($19,000, $3,800, 1897, 1923, 1958, 5 percent)
